source_text:
So I do have a question: codex-19's work is still very slow.  I've spent a good chunk of OpenAI/ChatGPT/Codex credits, initial balance 62,500 usage credits (a $2,500 USD value) on this project (26,353 credits remaining
), in addition to a week's usage allocation in one day.  This is not computationally easy work, but I really think that if we could accelerate the LISP side we'd improve our effeciency.  Codex-19 is working alone right now, I wonder what would happen if we backed off on the Python port and focused a team effort around catching the Lisp port up to where the Python port is now.  If we could do that then future work could go via the warm image path and would at least be faster, even if it still consumed the same amount of tokens

reply_text:
㊥ (backing off Python for a Lisp push) I agree with slowing the Python port, but I'd point the team at codex-18's transpiler, not codex-19's native rewrite. The Lisp side has 6k of the Python port's 164k lines ported or tested. Rewriting the rest by hand, one row at a time, would mean deriving every behaviour from Lean a second time. The transpiler instead converts the Python port mechanically, so its work grows with the number of Python features, not with the number of Lean declarations. Before committing credits, I'd ask codex-18 one cheap question: how far is the transpiled port from running `ParserFn.run` in a warm SBCL image, and how much faster is it on the slowest module? Shall I put that question to them, or will you, since you're in their buffer?

㊬ (numbers I checked) From `lisp/port-status.json`:

| Status | Modules | Lines |
|---|---|---|
| not ported | 644 | 148k |
| partial | 30 | 11.9k |
| differential-tested in some form | 14 | 3.8k |

`lisp-rows.json` still has `Array.extract` as the only current row. Its blocker is the numeral target type in `hAdd j 1`. Over the last 24 hours, codex-18 made 365 commits, codex-19 made 225 and codex-20 made 24.

🈖 (why the native route is hard to speed up) codex-19's last ten commits were match scoping, coverage, default instances and numerals. The Python port already went through each of these against Lean, and I reviewed the same bugs on both sides tonight. Much of that work is shared machinery, which more agents can't split up well. Each new row then depends on whatever the earlier rows built.

🈖 (why the transpiler route parallelises) The transpiler's own docs are organised by Python feature: `dataclass` fields, `lru_cache`, `contextvars`, string helpers, exception subclasses, and so on. Each feature can be one agent's job, and the agents rarely touch each other's code. There is a single milestone to measure progress by: the transpiled port running `ParserFn.run` and producing `types.py` with sha `fab1ef5d…`. After that, a Python fix is transpiled and rerun warm, and the cold probes that cost 20–30 minutes tonight largely go away.

㊟ (what I don't know)
- How close the transpiled port is to that milestone. Commit 1372973 is "Capture current startup dictionary items failure", which suggests it is failing at startup, but I can't tell the distance from here.
- Whether SBCL is actually faster on this workload. The transpiled code calls through a runtime that emulates Python semantics (`py-call`), which costs time compared with native Lisp. Timing one heavy module before scaling up would settle it.

Separately: on the Python side, warm reruns take 100–150 s against 1200–1900 s cold. Iterating warm and keeping cold runs for acceptance would cut some cost now, with no porting at all.

㊭ (order, if the answer is good)
1. Python: let the three jobs in flight finish (psw-default3, psw-sigma5, psw-proj3; two of them are discovery only) and dispatch no new ones.
2. codex-18 leads the transpiler push, with 2 more seats, one Python feature per job, measured against the `ParserFn.run` milestone.
3. codex-19 pauses `Array.extract` once their current commit lands and joins that team. Their native work stays as the reference for faithfulness.

🈳 (your call) Who asks codex-18, and which seats join if the answer is good?

previous_reply_acts.text: (codex-18 Lean proof) Good, I'll leave that thread to you and codex-18. If they want a second target later, codex-19's coverage checker (8692d86) has a short soundness statement, and I've already read its interval arithmetic. Their receipts in `lisp/curriculum/array-extract/{match-coverage,planner-coverage}/` would give the proof its test cases.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (proof claims) Please pass on one thing for when codex-18 reports results. A proof says the Lisp matches the Python only on the fragment its semantics models. That makes it worth knowing which constructs the proof's Python semantics leaves out, because the transpiler's output on those carries no guarantee.
